title: Structurally Aligned Subtask-Level Memory for Software Engineering Agents
claim: Retrieving past experience by whole-task similarity misleads on look-alike tasks; matching stage-level subtask intents reuses relevant experience even across dissimilar tasks.
layout: 2 stacked panels split by dashed line, left current task, right memory stack
description: The figure has two horizontal panels separated by a dashed gray line. The top panel shows instance-level memory. A blue 'Current Task: Fix Login Button' card on the left connects through a yellow arrow labeled 'High Global Similarity' to a stacked teal card, 'Fix Login Timeout', on the right. The teal card lists 'Check DB Logs' and 'Restart SQL'. A red arrow with a red X between the two cards shows the retrieval is wrong. The bottom panel shows subtask-level memory. The current task is broken into a flow of ANALYZE, REPRODUCE, EDIT and VERIFY steps. The stacked memory card 'Modify Search Bar' on the right holds purple subtask boxes with the same stage labels. The cards are linked by 'Low Global Similarity' and 'High Subtask Similarity'. The EDIT step is highlighted with yellow dashed outlines and a teal arrow with a green check mark. caption: Comparison of Instance-Level vs. Subtask-Level Memory. Top: Instance-level memory relies on global task similarity, causing reasoning interference when tasks share surface goals but require different reasoning logic. Bottom: Our method retrieves by matching stage-consistent subtask intents, enabling precise experience reuse even across globally dissimilar tasks.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant potential as autonomous software engineering (SWE) agents. Recent work has further explored augmenting these agents with memory mechanisms to support long-horizon reasoning. However, these approaches typically operate at a coarse instance granularity, treating the entire problem-solving episode as the atomic unit of storage and retrieval. We empirically demonstrate that instance-level memory suffers from a fundamental granularity mismatch, resulting in misguided retrieval when tasks with similar surface descriptions require distinct reasoning logic at specific stages. To address this, we propose Structurally Aligned Subtask-Level Memory, a method that aligns memory storage, retrieval, and updating with the agent's functional decomposition. Extensive experiments on SWE-bench Verified demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms both vanilla agents and strong instance-level memory baselines across diverse backbones, improving mean Pass@1 over the vanilla agent by +4.7 pp on average (e.g., +6.8 pp on Gemini 2.5 Pro). Performance gains grow with more interaction steps, showing that leveraging past experience benefits long-horizon reasoning in complex software engineering tasks.
